rationale: Over 453 held-out CONFLICTS items in four prompt configurations, mean confidence on wrong answers stays flat at 0.56-0.58 (max 0.96-1.00, mean prob gap -0.48 to -0.50) and correct/wrong confidence separation is only 0.073-0.166; authors judge confidence too weak to gate automation (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4).

Best configuration reaches 65.3% accuracy (macro-F1 0.559), matching the best zero-shot LLM reported in the source benchmark paper (Gemini 2.5 Flash 65.3%, literature comparator), but only with detailed label definitions (simple prompt 49.4%) and misinformation-class F1 0.08-0.20 (Sec. 3.1-3.2).

No typed decision model is measured; the paper defines five harness assurance properties and finds a real P4 scope-enforcement gap in the author's own NeuroSploit harness, i.e. evidence that scope enforcement belongs to harness code, not to model judgement (abstract; Sec. IX).

Swapping yes/no option names over fixed definitions flips 76.9% of Laya decisions vs 6.5% for 0/1 names (+70.4 pp, 95% CI 67.6-73.1) and inverts AUC 93.8%->23.2%; hosted Jev flips 32.5% (AUC 81.5%->58.1%, test-retest <=1.33%) and Open-Jev 19.5%, with 0% type errors throughout (Sec. 4.1, 4.5; Tables 1, 6).

KITE runs 1M agents x 20 steps in 0.9 s and passes content-fidelity gates in all 15 new countries, but intervention effects need sparse flagship-LLM anchors (Epstein effect MAE 0.0305->0.0180) and the preregistered primary policy-value gain was not shown (hybrid minus kernel 0.0027 [-0.0118, 0.0169]) (abstract; Sec. 5; Table D1).

Probability thresholds become usable only after task-specific isotonic recalibration on a holdout (Jev ECE 0.1235->0.0077; open NLI 0.1072->0.0063); the authors recommend calibration on the intended data before thresholding (Sec. 5.6; App. G).

One-question Jev evaluator reaches Kendall tau 0.573 (RadEvalX) and 0.398 (RadEvalExpert) with expert error counts, beating an open NLI judge, and detects false negation with AUROC 0.977, but the local LLM-based RadMatch agrees better on clinically significant errors in both expert datasets (abstract; Sec. 5.1-5.3).

Raw sentence-level ECE is 0.1192 (holdout ECE 0.1235) versus 0.1045 for the open NLI baseline on 19,513 ReXErr examples, and becomes 0.0077 only after isotonic recalibration on a holdout (Sec. 5.6; App. G).

On Jev's 12 most confident errors per ordinal panel, 242/252 LLM verdicts (96.0%) repeat the wrong answer vs 50.3% expected under independence, and with cross-fitted thresholds no Jev->LLM cascade beats the best single judge by more than 1.5 points (2.0 with oracle thresholds, n.s.), trailing it on 6 of 9 panels (Sec. 5.3, 6.2; Tables 3-4).

Across 9 panels from 7 human-labelled benchmarks, Jev's accuracy differs significantly from flash-tier LLM judges in at most 8 of 27 paired comparisons, ahead mostly on binary checklist criteria and behind only on ordinal ones, at 16-325x lower cost (abstract; Sec. 4.1-4.2; Table 3).

Jev's probabilities are calibrated on the binary panels, but its confidence ranks its own errors only weakly on ordinal panels (error-detection AUROC 0.57-0.70 on six, 0.49 on ELLIPSE) (Sec. 6; Table 3).

Repository mining of 2,170 public Jev projects (1,865 created in the first week) shows broad adoption across 8 domains, but Safety & Governance is 175 projects (8.1%) with about 3.5% of stars while routing/automation holds 41.4% of stars; labels assigned by LLM agents (Table 1; Sec. 2).

Secondary evidence review of 28 papers (19-24 Sep 2026): the typed readout has not shown an independent accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts, gains are mainly latency and cost, and only 1 of 27 papers passes the option-name test; a review, so excluded from tallies to avoid double counting (abstract; Finding 1; Table 6).

On 480 negation pairs Jev's P(X)+P(not X) misses 1 by 0.064 (95% CI 0.055-0.072) vs 0.293 for Qwen3.8-27B first-token and 0.122 verbalized, but Jev is still incoherent: violations about 5x its repeat-noise floor (0.013) and single-label probabilities summing to 1.14 (abstract; Sec. 5.1-5.2).

Author-built 9B 'System One' scorer (SubJudge, digit-token readout) achieves the lowest individual MAE on PluriHarms (0.1659 vs 0.168 Kimi-K3) and beats frontier LLMs on iNews arousal/dominance, but no group-fairness or wording/order stability test is reported and Jev is not tested (Sec. 3.1; Tables 1-2).

SubJudge matches or surpasses frontier LLMs on several personalised-judgement metrics (PluriHarms aggregated MAE 0.2278 vs 0.228 GPT-5.4; iNews arousal MAE 0.7530 vs 0.8929) with 1.29-261x lower latency than Qwen3.5-9B, but not on every metric (e.g. iNews valence) (abstract; Sec. 3.1; Table 2).

Jev is the best typed model on R-Judge (AUROC 0.961 vs Laya 0.533) and AgentHarm and comparable to GPT-4.1, but all five reasoning judges have higher R-Judge Macro-F1 and Jev misses all 130 no-EI implicit injections on WAInjectBench (Sec. 4.2, 5.2; Tables 6-8).
Jev misses all 130 WAInjectBench injections without explicit instructions, assigning unsafe probability <0.1, with 130 false negatives at confidence >=0.95 (Sec. 4.2, 5.2).

Under the strictest error limits symmetric policies automate nothing on WAInjectBench and 7.63% on R-Judge; separate thresholds reach 47.03% mainly through blocks (110 blocks, 1 allow), passing confirmation does not ensure limits hold on test, and LLM judges catch at most 5 of Jev's 130 high-confidence misses (Sec. 5.3-5.4).

Fine-tuned Laya-322M reaches 98.85% accuracy and 0.42% FPR on the 607-item clean Chinese DUCS-Bench split, but untuned Laya has 35.71% FPR and fine-tuning lowers SafetyBench-ZH accuracy 60.33%->56.81% unless 458-item replay is mixed in (65.05%) (Table II; Table V; Sec. IV-F).

Validation-tuned CPU->NPU confidence cascade achieves 99.23% accuracy, 0.00% FPR and 41.63 ms mean latency, but only on a 130-query live slice and with gating thresholds and fine-tuning fitted to the authors' own domain (Sec. IV-D; Table III).

On 5,219 agent trajectories Jev's benchmark-averaged positive-class F1 is 77.8 vs 74.1 for the best generative judge GLM-5.2 (paired difference 2.7 points, exploratory bootstrap 95% CI 0.5-4.8) at a common threshold, though GLM leads on 2 of 4 benchmarks and is more precise (91.9 vs 77.1) (abstract; Table 2; App. B).

PACT training on an open single-token typed model lowers answer flips under answer-code relabelling to 9.8% vs 13.8% for the published Nimble recipe and 23.5% for the base model on a frozen 324-item holdout over three seeds, reducing but not removing the bias (abstract; results table, Sec. VI).

Against a seed-matched cross-entropy-only control PACT lowers NLL by 26% and halves seed spread, with calibration relying on a fitted three-parameter contextual temperature; accuracy is not raised over the published recipe (84.6 vs 85.2%) (abstract; Sec. VI).

Across 738,164 live Choice answers the returned confidence equals (p_max-1/N)/(1-1/N) within mean residual 0.005, so it rescales top probability and rises with padded options (formula-derived: 0.20 at N=2 to 0.58 at N=20 for p_max 0.60, not an observed manipulation); identical repeated calls moved confidence 0.84-0.88 and flipped labels on a flat question (7 vs 2 of 9) (Sec. 1; Table 2).

Statistical argument (no new data) that calibration is a property of model and data distribution, so vendor calibration need not transfer to a user's production data; recommends treating Jev outputs as scores and recalibrating (e.g. Platt scaling on a few hundred labels).

In a 13-run reproduction of Laya's RLCD fine-tune (three seeds for main arms), the RL term makes inference over-sharp (fitted binary temperature 1.16->1.72 and NLL 0.871->0.928 as noise rises 0.5->2) and CE-only matches or beats RL+CE on every proper score; calibration comes from distillation plus temperature scaling (report abstract; Sec. VI; Tables III, V).

Jev rejects all 6,336 directed racial-superiority claims (mean P(true) about 3%), but when forced to name one group White receives 51.12% of first picks and wins 6 of 8 traits, with gender picks also stereotyped; option order was not counterbalanced, so a position effect is possible (Figs. 1-2, 5).

With structural receiving checks, the Jev semantic gate withheld all 12 unsupported releases on 48 synthetic episodes, but on 120 VitaminC pairs it accepted 1 of 120 benchmark-negatives (confidence 1.00) and withheld 38 of 120 positives (label agreement 194/240, 80.8%), so autonomous reliability is not established (ADDENDUM.md; rr-jev-vitamin-c/RESULTS.md).

The note frames the pilot as mechanism evidence only: PASS as a reproducible experiment, ESCALATE for legal conclusions, BLOCK for real files or automated decisions; no auditability of decisions is measured (Estado section).

On 30 public Argentine Supreme Court metadata records Jev classified legal area correctly in 60% (Kev 20%) versus 96.7% for deterministic rules, and procedural vehicle in 96.7% versus rules 100% (Resultados table).
At confidence >=0.90 Jev's legal-area answer was correct in only 12 of 16 cases, with errors at confidence 0.99 and 1.00 (Resultados).
Argmax was stable across six option orders in 93.3% of cases for both Jev and Kev (n=30) (Resultados table).

Normative essay arguing that removing natural-language reasoning traces weakens audit, responsibility attribution and alignment-faking detection, and that calibration is not logical reliability; no data (Sec. 2-4).

Single calls on 6 states: Noul probabilities put conflict (0.50-0.57) and ignorance (0.46-0.48) in one band, but a Choice schema naming both states separated the four conflict/ignorance cases with probability 1.0 (controls also correct), binary Choice showed a directional bias (0.67-0.85 toward red), and Score separated the extremes (2.04 vs 3.95); the author disclaims collapse per se (Tables 2-5; Sec. 7-8).

Methods note proposing source-separated, participant-reviewed Choice/Score/Noul question proposals with provenance; only 14/14 synthetic software-contract tests passed and no live Jev call was evaluated (abstract; Sec. 5, 7).
Design requires human review and participant final decision before any execution, but the note states that oversight effects, harms and Jev outputs were not measured (Sec. 4.5, 7).

With 2-3 equally eligible machines Jev gave dominant probability to the first one introduced in the context (NEXA 93%, ZEXA 86%, KELT 84%) and the preference followed context-order reversal (AORA 90%) while answer-option reversal barely moved it (92%); exploratory single runs on synthetic items (Sec. 4.10-4.15).
With no eligible option Jev put 83% on an ineligible machine, but when an explicit 'none satisfies' option was added it chose it, so abstention works only if the schema offers it (Sec. 4.6-4.7).

The open Laya judge (laya 0.3.4) is near-perfect when the answer is explicit (0.9909, n=220) but collapses on absent evidence (no_support 0.3091, n=220) where the generative LLM scores 1.00, reaches 0.4583 vs 1.00 on authority location and 0.225 vs 0.75-0.90 on 77-class intent, and its errors do not complement the LLM's (judge-only correct 0-2 vs LLM-only 23-27) (abstract; Sec. 6.1, 7).

Self-reported fields (truncated, fits, probability, band) were wrong or misleading, e.g. 'probability' is P(selected option) and flips every 'false' answer, but the paper attributes them to access layers (third-party wrapper and plugin), not the engines; provider-returned probabilities and confidence were not shown untrustworthy (Sec. 3.1.1; Results B 3.4-3.8).
On 1,100 binary items Laya's ECE is 0.2259 vs 0.0028 for the LLM and its Brier 0.2571 is worse than a constant predictor's 0.2400, despite AUC 0.7136 (95% CI 0.682-0.745) (abstract; Sec. 6.2).

On a prespecified 204-item holdout a Laya >=0.90 gate avoided 60.8% of phi4:14b calls with cascade accuracy 181/204 vs 180/204 for phi4 (+0.5 pp, 95% CI -2.5 to +3.9), meeting all criteria, but the threshold was chosen on a pilot and all 8 accepted errors bypassed escalation (Sec. 3.2-3.3).

Laya multilingual's observed accuracy was below its mean confidence in every band (e.g. 0.90-0.95: 73% accuracy vs 92.9% confidence; >=0.95: 96.3% vs 99.2%), consistent with documented over-confidence of raw outputs (Sec. 3.5).

Against Kev-0.8B the strongest of 15 attacks flipped 5/45 action-gate (11%, 95% CI 2-24%) and 12/45 investment decisions (27%, 11-44%); confidence fell for almost any added text, so the model did not recognise attacks (Sec. 5.2-5.4).

A coverage-matched threshold sent every attacked wrong answer to review (0/90, upper bound 3.3%) and a fixed 0.8 gate passed none as served, but at raw T=1 three attacked errors passed 0.8; protection was a side effect of confidence dropping and attacks forced reviews and false blocks (36/46 safe commands flipped) (Sec. 5.2, 5.5, 6.1).
